articles.title: Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important?
articles.summary: The BBC's Frank Gardner explains why the narrow waterway is key to oil transportation and the world economy.
articles.body:
Thousands of refugees have fled Yemen in recent days after Iran-backed Houthis seized territory along the country's Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa.

The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

Now, following a Saudi request, the UK has said it will deploy a military aircraft to help refuel Saudi Arabian fighter jets taking part in "purely defensive" missions.

The BBC's Frank Gardner has this analysis.

articles.title: AP Exclusive: ICE hides locations of thousands of detainees with final removal orders
articles.summary: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has stopped publicly revealing where it is holding thousands of detainees who are subject to final deportation order...
articles.body:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has stopped publicly revealing where it is holding thousands of detainees who are subject to final deportation orders , an unannounced move that has made it far more difficult for lawyers and relatives to find them, according to current and former officials familiar with the practice.

ICE removed those detainees from its online detainee locator system on Sept. 15, according to three current and former ICE officials who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the change. Several lawyers contacted by The Associated Press confirmed their clients vanished from the system this week, and the American Immigration Lawyers Association warned its members about the situation Friday.

The move represents a stark departure from previous practice and highlights the hardline nature of President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown, leaving thousands of detainees exceedingly hard to trace and potentially unable to exercise all of their legal options.

The practice, which applies to detainees who have received final orders of removal from an immigration court , could speed deportations by making last-minute legal challenges harder to pursue, immigration lawyers said. Nearly 16,000 people who were arrested and booked into ICE detention in July were subject to final removal orders, more than a third of the overall bookings, according to ICE data obtained by the Deportation Data Project based at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA.

The practice does not apply to detainees held at a detention facility in Adelanto, California or at temporary holding facilities in Minneapolis, New York City or suburban Chicago, the sources said. Judges have ordered ICE to list detainees in those facilities in the online locator promptly upon their arrival, as part of litigation over their detention practices.

Lawyers and relatives distressed by lack of information on detainees

The effort to hide their locations adds to the ways in which the Trump administration has made life harder for detainees and their families as it has increased pressure on them to waive appeals and agree to deportation.

ICE did not publicize the move and in a statement issued to the AP, the agency did not confirm or deny it. The statement said detainees with final removal orders were being prioritized for deportation, even as ICE faces a "historic number of injunctions" from courts stopping individual removals.

As a result of the change, lawyers and relatives lost track of their clients and loved ones without explanation, which is especially concerning because detainees are frequently moved to new facilities before deportation, said Greg Chen, senior director of government relations at the American Immigration Lawyers Association.

"Families are freaking out because they think the person has been deported and they don't know where the person might be," he said. "On the attorney side, this has serious implications for the ability to contact their client. It certainly has implications about how it will interfere with the attorney-client relationship."

The Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent agency, has argued that people who are subject to final removal orders have received due process. That usually means an immigration judge has ordered their removal after a hearing, including cases when immigrants fail to show up, and the decision was affirmed on appeal or not appealed.

Detainees with final removal orders still have options to appeal

Still, those detainees have options to challenge their detention and removal, including seeking to reopen the case or by bringing what's known as a habeas petition asking a judge to release them on constitutional grounds. Federal judges have granted thousands of rulings ordering that detainees be released or granted bond hearings.

ICE detention facilities held more than 65,000 people as of early July, the most recent available data. Around 30% of them likely have final removal orders, said Michelle Mendez, legal director at the National Immigration Project.

More people have been issued final removal orders after failing to show up for hearings in recent months because the administration's immigration courts have taken steps to make it harder to participate and to reopen such cases, she said.

"To me, it's just another iteration of disappearing people," she said. "Why would we do that in the United States of America? It's something we'd hear about in another country and be concerned about individual rights and due process."

Some with final removal orders also have legal protections against deportation to their countries of origin based on the likelihood they would be tortured or persecuted. Many of them are facing removal to third-party countries where they have no ties and their disappearance in ICE's system will make legal challenges harder, lawyers said.

Lawyers say clients have vanished from ICE locator system

ICE initiated the online detainee locator system in 2010 to allow relatives, lawyers and the public to search for people in custody. Previously they had to call ICE regional offices or individual facilities to try to track them down.

Many advocates and lawmakers have complained that the system updates too slowly and contains too much inaccurate or missing information, allowing ICE to shield the locations of detainees for days or weeks. Minors, people who have been held by U.S. Customs and Border Protection for less than 48 hours, and detainees who are being transported are not in the system, among others.

But the exclusion of detainees with final removal orders has no apparent parallel, several immigration lawyers said. Atenas Burrola Estrada, a deputy program director with the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, said that "every single one of our clients who has a final order has disappeared from the locator," including 17 in all as of Monday.

Among those disappeared from the locator system are eight Somali men being detained at the U.S. military base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, according to one of their attorneys, My Khanh Ngo, of the American Civil Liberties Union. She said the change could make it "nearly impossible" for people to challenge their removals in some cases.

"If you can't find your client, don't know what's happening to your client, you can't get that information to the court to stop their removal," she said.

articles.title: Dog Side-Eyes the Human in Her Backseat Like He’s Sitting in First Class Without a Ticket

articles.body:
A video of a dog named Koda giving a human passenger side-eye in the backseat has gone viral on Instagram with over 68K likes.

The pet parent uploaded the video on September 19, showing Koda's adorable and hilarious reaction to sharing the backseat with a human.

The dog's side-eye and disapproving look at the human sitting beside her has left the internet laughing and commenting on the humorous video.

Fur babies can have certain traits that are adorable and super funny at the same time. This video captured a cute dog named Koda side-eyeing the human who was sharing the backseat with her, as if the individual was sitting in first class without a ticket. On September 19, the pet parent recently uploaded the video on their Instagram account. Since then, the clip has gone viral, garnering more than 68K likes on Instagram at the time of writing.

Dog gives a human passenger side-eye when she has to share the backseat

A funny video on Instagram showed an adorable dog named Koda giving a human passenger side-eye when she had to share the backseat with the person. The video has left the internet in stitches, as people can't get enough of the dog's reaction to the human sitting beside her in the backseat. In the caption, the pet parent humorously wrote, "So unfair."

The Instagram video began by giving a closer look at the backseat of the car. The dog was already sitting in the backseat when a human entered the car and sat on the seat right beside her. In the meantime, the text written over the clip read, "My dog when she has to share the backseat."

The fur baby continued giving proper side-eye to the human in the car. The dog's reaction was super adorable and hilarious. Sharing the backseat with someone clearly did not sit well with her. The video will make anybody laugh.

In the comments section of the video, one admirer wrote, "She's beautiful! But also that look of "can you just GO?!" has me cackling." Meanwhile, another fan's comment read, "As a single child, that's me when I have to share anything." "She's not pupset, she's just disappointed," added another admirer.

articles.title: Workday expands its India operations
articles.summary: Workday is expanding its Chennai GCC into a key engineering hub for agentic AI, with 1,600 employees in India, 1,800 customers, and a focus on data sovereignty.
articles.body: Chennai: Workday, the US-based HR and financial software company, has expanded its Chennai centre into a key engineering hub as it develops agentic AI systems. The company has also ramped up its India presence in recent months and now has around 1,500 employees in the country.Its Chennai capability centre has around 600 employees, who work with global teams on critical product development.Max Wessel, SVP, Product at Workday, said the company’s development teams have “clear and complete missions” and are responsible for core products rather than outsourced work.“Our engineering teams in Chennai have taken the reins of some of our agentic development, model context protocol (MCP) surfaces and agent skills. We also have a team owning the core of our financial system, global spend and tax capabilities,” he said.Workday has also expanded its local commercial operations to serve around 1,800 customers. A key focus is supporting global capability centres (GCCs) of US-headquartered multinationals, along with non-US MNCs and Indian enterprises in professional services, technology and telecom, and financial services.Wessel described India as one of Workday’s most strategic bets and said revenue growth in the country is expected to outpace the company’s overall global growth for years, without giving specific projections.To support regulated sectors such as financial services and meet growing demand from customers, Workday is focusing on data sovereignty and local infrastructure hosting.The company is also using its unified application architecture to enable AI-driven autonomous workflows, while adopting new pricing models, including flex credits. articles.title: Homem é condenado a 30 anos de prisão por matar rapaz em Caraguatatuba | G1
articles.standfirst: Júri reconheceu motivo fútil e ataque de surpresa. Crime teria sido motivado por ciúmes da namorada.
articles.summary: Júri reconheceu motivo fútil e ataque de surpresa. Crime teria sido motivado por ciúmes da namorada.
articles.body:
Homem é condenado a 30 anos de prisão por matar rapaz a tiros em Caraguatatuba — Foto: Reprodução

Um homem de 26 anos foi condenado a 30 anos e 4 meses de prisão pelo assassinato de um rapaz, em Caraguatatuba , no Litoral Norte de São Paulo. O resultado do julgamento foi divulgado nesta segunda-feira (21).

Segundo a denúncia do Ministério Público, o crime aconteceu em 16 de março de 2024, na Rua Amparo, no bairro Perequê-Mirim. A vítima foi atingida por disparos de arma de fogo e morreu no local.

A acusação sustentou que o crime teria sido motivado pela suspeita de que a vítima estaria tentando se envolver com a namorada do réu. Ainda segundo a denúncia, o homem teria encontrado a vítima e efetuado os disparos durante uma discussão.

O júri reconheceu a autoria do crime e rejeitou o pedido de absolvição apresentado pela defesa. Os jurados também consideraram que o homicídio foi cometido por motivo fútil e com recurso que dificultou a defesa da vítima, qualificadoras que aumentaram a pena.

Na sentença, o juiz fixou a pena em 30 anos e 4 meses de reclusão, em regime fechado. O magistrado também determinou que o réu não poderá recorrer em liberdade e manteve a prisão preventiva.

Durante o julgamento, a defesa sustentou a negativa de autoria e pediu a absolvição do acusado. O Ministério Público, por outro lado, pediu a condenação pelo homicídio qualificado.

De acordo com a denúncia, na tarde de 16 de março de 2024, a vítima foi atingida por dois disparos, um no tórax e outro na região da nuca. Três estojos de munição calibre 7,65 foram encontrados nas proximidades.

A investigação apontou que o acusado teria se apossado de uma arma e ido ao encontro da vítima após uma discussão ocorrida no dia anterior. Segundo a acusação, a vítima tentou fugir, mas foi atingida pelas costas.

articles.title: Trump promete extinguir 'interferência' no Hemisfério Ocidental | G1
articles.standfirst: Discurso do presidente dos EUA na Assembleia Geral da ONU nesta terça (22) ocorre em meio a uma grave crise enfrentada pela organização multilateral, em parte incentivada por ele próprio.
articles.summary: Discurso do presidente dos EUA na Assembleia Geral da ONU nesta terça (22) ocorre em meio a uma grave crise enfrentada pela organização multilateral, em parte incentivada por ele próprio.
articles.body:
O presidente dos Estados Unidos , Donald Trump , prometeu extinguir o que chamou de "interferência externa" no Hemisfério Ocidental e que pode utilizar o poderio militar norte-americano para isso, em discurso nesta terça-feira (22) na Assembleia Geral da ONU , em Nova York.

Trump, que busca dominar e expulsar a presença dos rivais China e Rússia do Hemisfério Ocidental , disse em seu discurso que busca "acabar com décadas de violência, instabilidade e interferência estrangeira" na região, e que utilizará "poderio militar incomparável" para atingir esse objetivo —utilizando a operação contra Nicolás Maduro como exemplo.

"Nossas ações na Venezuela são uma prova de que não permitiremos mais que ameaças contra os Estados Unidos criem uma base de apoio em qualquer lugar do Hemisfério Ocidental e, se necessário, usaremos nosso poderio militar incomparável para proteger nossos interesses nacionais vitais", afirmou.

O presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, discursa na 81ª Assembleia Geral das Nações Unidas na sede da ONU, na cidade de Nova York, EUA, em 22 de setembro de 2026 — Foto: Mike Segar/Reuters

O presidente norte-americano também comparou os cartéis de drogas ao grupo terrorista Estado Islâmico e afirmou que esses "grupos e gangues sangrentos" não afligirão mais os países do Ocidente.

" Lançamos o poder das Forças Armadas dos EUA para eliminar gangues e cartéis de drogas sangrentos. (...) Os cartéis são o Estado Islâmico do Hemisfério Ocidental. São inimigos em guerra contra a civilização, usando assassinato, estupro, tortura e extorsão como instrumentos de terror, e por isso eles devem ser mortos, exilados ou detidos", afirmou Trump.

O discurso de Trump ocorre em meio a uma grave crise enfrentada pela ONU, em parte incentivada pelo próprio líder norte-americano. Desde que ele retornou à Casa Branca, em janeiro de 2025, Trump não apenas criticou a instituição multilateral em diversas ocasiões como também criou um órgão internacional para rivalizar com a ONU, o "Conselho da Paz".

O presidente Lula, que discursou antes de Trump, afirmou disse que o Brasil "não é quintal de ninguém" e não vai "terceirizar a responsabilidade" de combater os grupos criminosos brasileiros —em referência à pressão da Casa Branca contra o PCC e o CV.

"Não precisamos de porta-aviões vigiando nossas águas", afirmou Lula, que acrescentou ter entregue uma proposta ao presidente dos EUA sobre o assunto.

Inclusive, num gesto que refletiu as atuais tensões diplomáticas entre Brasil e EUA, Lula não deu atenção ao Secretário de Estado norte-americano, Marco Rubio , no plenário da Assembleia Geral. Momentos após o discurso de Trump, Rubio foi até o presidente brasileiro, porém não conseguiu falar com ele.

As tensões entre Brasil e EUA decorrem das ameaças militares contra PCC e CV —designados organizações terroristas internacionais por Trump— e de tentativas de influenciar as eleições presidenciais brasileiras.

Esses elementos, inclusive, "viraram do avesso" a relação entre Lula e Trump, que desabrochava justamente na Assembleia Geral do ano passado, quando o líder dos EUA revelou ter encontrado brevemente com Lula e disse ter tido uma "química excelente" com o presidente brasileiro — relembre esse momento.

Ataque à ONU, ameaças ao Irã e acordo pela Groenlândia

O presidente norte-americano também criticou a ONU e suas agências. Ele chamou o Tribunal Penal Internacional (TPI), da ONU, de "fora de controle" e "maléfico" e pediu que todos todos os países-membros esvaziem a instituição.

Ele também acusou "os principais funcionários de Direitos Humanos da ONU" de criticar os EUA em busca de "mutilar crianças para as tornar transgêneros" e as políticas de imigração do governo Trump.

Durante sua fala, Trump também exaltou a situação interna dos EUA durante seu governo e afirmou que "o mundo inteiro está sendo levantado por um EUA energizados e mais poderosos do mundo".

Ele defendeu a guerra no Oriente Médio e reiterou que o Irã "nunca terá uma arma nuclear". Ele também ameaçou "aniquilar o Irã para o inferno" caso não haja acordo de paz após os midterms.

Trump também anunciou a construção de duas grandes bases militares dos EUA na Groenlândia após ter chegado a um acordo com a Dinamarca , que foi assinado no início da tarde desta terça.

"Ampliamos a presença dos EUA no Ártico e no Atlântico Norte, em um acordo que também protege muito a Europa e deixa a Otan mais forte do que nunca", afirmou Trump.

ONU se prepara para a 81ª Assembleia Geral das Nações Unidas — Foto: David Dee Delgado/Reuters

A Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU) enfrenta atualmente constates ataques contra sua legitimidade, cortes de verba e uma crise geral de credibilidade.

A crise, inclusive, tem até sugestões de dentro da própria ONU para que o órgão multilateral seja encolhido e "volte ao básico" para continuar existindo.

Diante do cenário, a ONU usará sua 81ª Assembleia Geral para fazer um apelo pela sua própria sobrevivência.

articles.title: VÍDEO: Rubio se aproxima de Lula no plenário da Assembleia Geral da ONU | G1
articles.standfirst: Imagens registraram secretário de Estado dos EUA, crítico de Lula, tentando se aproximar do presente brasileiro na sessão plenária no internvalo dos discurso de líderes na Assembleia Geral da ONU, em Nova York.
articles.summary: Imagens registraram secretário de Estado dos EUA, crítico de Lula, tentando se aproximar do presente brasileiro na sessão plenária no internvalo dos discurso de líderes na Assembleia Geral da ONU, em Nova York.
articles.body:
Crítico do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, o secretário de Estado dos Estados Unidos, Marco Rubio, tentou falar com o brasileiro durante a Assembleia Geral da Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU).

No intervalo dos discursos de líderes mundiais, enquanto diplomatas e chefes de governo se falavam nos corredores do plenário, Rubio foi até Lula, mas não conseguiu falar com o brasileiro.

Imagens registradas pela TV Globo flagraram o momento. Nelas, é possível ver que Rubio caminha em direção a Lula. Ele chegou perto do presidente brasileiro e apontou em sua direção. Lula olha rapidamente em direção a Rubio, mas continua a andar.

Brasil e Estados Unidos não têm encontros bilaterais previstos durante a Assembleia Geral da ONU neste ano. No ano passado, o presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, e Lula se encontraram nos bastidores, entre os discursos de ambos.

Momento em que o secretário de Estado dos EUA, Marco Rubio, se aproxima do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, durante a Assembleia Geral da ONU, em Nova York, em 22 de setembro de 2026. — Foto: Reprodução/ g1

Lula e Rubio já se criticaram mutuamente e trocaram ofensas. Lula já chamou Marco Rubio, um conservador filho de cubanos nascido na Flórida, de "latino-americano frustrado", enquanto o secretário norte-americano já acusou Lula de "se curvar diante da China" e de agir de má-fé.

Momento em que o secretário de Estado dos EUA, Marco Rubio, tenta falar com o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, na Assembleia Geral da ONU, em Nova York, em 22 de setembro de 2026. — Foto: Reprodução/ TV Globo

articles.title: Cantor Rick foi rara voz negra no topo do sertanejo; entenda o apagamento histórico no ritmo | G1
articles.standfirst: Cantor encontrado morto em SC relatou casos de racismo. Especialistas apontam que indústria musical embranqueceu raízes do gênero e mantém engrenagem que prejudica novos talentos.
articles.summary: Cantor encontrado morto em SC relatou casos de racismo. Especialistas apontam que indústria musical embranqueceu raízes do gênero e mantém engrenagem que prejudica novos talentos.
articles.body:
Rick e Renner durante apresentação no Vila Country, em São Paulo. — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram/RickeRenner

A confirmação da morte do cantor Rick , encontrado nesta terça-feira (22) após um acidente com helicóptero em Santa Catarina, marca a despedida de uma voz histórica da música popular brasileira. O fato lança luz sobre um dado estrutural do sertanejo. Rick era um dos poucos artistas negros a alcançar o estrelato no estilo. O gênero domina rádios e plataformas de streaming há anos, mas os rankings de sucesso são quase totalmente brancos.

É preciso voltar a 1996 para encontrar a última vez que um representante negro figurou no top 10 das rádios com música sertaneja. Naquele ano, João Paulo e Daniel ocuparam a terceira posição. O próprio João Paulo, morto no ano seguinte, enfrentava o preconceito de perto. Executivos do mercado chegaram a sugerir que Daniel trocasse de parceiro no início da carreira para formar uma dupla de cantores brancos, sob a justificativa de que a formação faria mais sentido comercialmente.

Rick conhecia essa realidade. Ao lado de Renner, lidou com episódios de racismo. Em um caso relatado por ele, uma fã se recusou a tirar foto com o cantor por não gostar de negros. A situação levou o parceiro a comprar a briga e recusar a foto.

O sertanejo também guardava histórias do amigo João Paulo. Uma delas envolvia um contratante de elite que afirmou que o show não teria sido comprado se ele soubesse da presença de um homem negro na dupla.

Apagamento histórico e estética excludente

Para Luiz Antonio Guerra, doutor em Sociologia pela Universidade de São Paulo, a ausência de nomes negros na música sertaneja é reflexo do apagamento das raízes negras da música caipira.

João Paulo, Rick e Kleo Dibah — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

A partir da década de 1930, a intelectualidade paulista e a indústria iniciaram uma modernização que excluiu essas influências do gênero, restringindo o estilo à moda de viola e ao cateretê. Expressões musicais negras foram separadas e associadas exclusivamente ao samba carioca ou à música nordestina.

Para o jornalista André Piunti, especialista em música sertaneja, a modernização e a indústria fonográfica estão entre as culpadas pelo embranquecimento do sertanejo. "Quando a música passa a fazer parte da indústria que coloca o LP na gôndola da loja, que leva o artista para as televisões, ou que faz a dupla rodar fisicamente para conhecer os locais, as gravadoras e alguns executivos já cortavam por serem negros."

Rick, parceiro de Renner, revelou que passou por muitas situações de racismo. "A gente viveu situações delicadas. Eu vivi, sim, situações de preconceito", disse o cantor no canal de Piunti no YouTube, citando o dia em que uma fã foi ao show da dupla e pediu uma foto para Renner. Na hora em que o cantor chamou Rick para se juntar ao clique, a mulher disse "que não gostava de negros". Renner recusou o pedido da foto.

A "modernização" do sertanejo foi um sinônimo de embranquecimento estético e mercadológico. Quando o estilo passou a exigir a imagem dos artistas em capas de discos e vitrines, executivos de gravadoras barravam a contratação de pessoas negras.

A imposição era tão intensa que ícones absolutos do gênero, como Tião Carreiro, passaram por um clareamento visual nas capas de seus projetos para que o produto fosse melhor aceito nas vendas. O mesmo ocorreu com Cascatinha & Inhana nos anos 1950. Eles estouraram nas rádios em uma época em que o público consumia os sucessos sem conhecer o rosto dos intérpretes.

Rejeição à militância e o peso de um hit

A Tião Carreiro & Pardinho desde a infância — Foto: Reprodução

Superar essa barreira exige enfrentar um mercado que rejeita discursos sociais. O sertanejo é caracterizado por ser um ambiente resistente a militâncias. Tentativas de emplacar movimentos de conscientização racial encontram forte oposição da indústria. Sem espaço para o debate direto, a própria obra de grandes ídolos do passado reproduzia o racismo velado da época, a exemplo da faixa "Preto de alma branca", sucesso de Tião Carreiro.

Nesse cenário de proporções desleais, onde há dezenas de artistas brancos tentando o estrelato para cada cantor negro, a única via de ascensão comprovada é o sucesso estrondoso de uma música. O mercado fonográfico foca no desempenho orgânico da canção. Especialistas apontam que a mudança estrutural só ganhará força quando um artista negro furar a bolha com uma faixa de alcance nacional. Esse movimento serviria como espelho para puxar uma fila de novos talentos, em uma dinâmica semelhante à que Marília Mendonça liderou para as mulheres no feminejo.

Sem essa figura central de grande visibilidade, as novas gerações não se reconhecem no ritmo e o ciclo de exclusão continua. Nomes em ascensão, como Junior Marques, David Henrique e Diogo Henrique, buscam o espaço que João Paulo, Pena Branca & Xavantinho e o próprio Rick abriram a duras penas. Junior Marques já chegou a dividir palco com Gusttavo Lima em festivais recentes. A morte de Rick deixa o mainstream sertanejo ainda menos diverso.

articles.title: Mississippi grand jury declines to indict anyone in death of 18-year-old who vanished in coastal waters
articles.summary: A 23-member Jackson County grand jury heard from 43 witnesses and found Nolan Wells' death on Horn Island was consistent with drowning, not foul play.
articles.body: A Mississippi grand jury found no evidence of criminal conduct in the death of 18-year-old Nolan Wells, concluding that the college football player’s body was found under circumstances "consistent with drowning" after his disappearance during a Fourth of July boating trip. The 23-member Jackson County grand jury found no criminal charges were warranted after hearing from 43 witnesses and reviewing physical and digital evidence, police reports, interviews, videos, images and maps, according to the grand jury report released by District Attorney Angel Myers McIlrath on Monday. Wells disappeared July 4 after traveling with friends to Horn Island, a barrier island off Mississippi’s Gulf Coast. His body was recovered in the waters off the island two days later after a multi-agency search. NEW AUDIO RELEASED FOLLOWING NOLAN WELLS DISAPPEARANCE DOESN'T SHOW 'ANYTHING NEFARIOUS': RETIRED FBI AGENT The report said the "position of, condition of, time of discovery, and location" of Wells’ body were consistent with drowning and that there was "no credible evidence" anyone traveling to or from the island committed a crime related to his death. The grand jury also found that bruising on the back of Wells’ head was "not a fatal injury." The report said there was no evidence of a fatal injury or organic disease, though investigators could not determine how Wells suffered the bruise. One witness testified that Wells was seen slipping "awkwardly off the side of a boat" around the time he was last seen. The witness could not say whether Wells struck his head during the fall and said Wells continued socializing afterward and did not appear injured. The report also said Wells was not involved in a physical altercation or argument that day. SHARPTON OFFERS $50K FOR NOLAN WELLS CASE ARREST WITH LAWYER TO RELEASE AUTOPSY AT NAACP A private autopsy commissioned by Wells’ family had previously listed his cause and manner of death as "undetermined pending investigation." During a July 22 news conference, civil rights attorney Ben Crump said the examination found an area of "red discoloration" on the back of Wells’ head, but pathologist Dr. Roger Mitchell could not determine a cause or manner of death. Questions had also been raised about Wells’ alcohol consumption. A July 5 Mississippi Department of Marine Resources Marine Patrol email previously obtained by Fox News Digital listed Wells’ alcohol intake as "heavy" while authorities searched for him. The email did not identify the source of that information. The grand jury found that Wells bought alcohol using a fake ID and that no adults of legal drinking age provided him with alcohol on the island. The report said toxicology testing was "not particularly informative" because decomposition fluid is an unreliable source for determining substance levels in a body. It also said there was no cocaine in Wells’ system and no evidence he had ever used the drug. The report also shed light on Wells’ cellphone, which was taken back to the mainland without him. CAJUN NAVY LEADER WARNS NOLAN WELLS' SEARCH AREA HAS DEADLY 'WASHING MACHINE' CURRENTS: 'LOTS OF DROWNINGS' The grand jury said it was not unusual for people visiting the island to return on different boats or leave phones and other belongings aboard boats while socializing. Wells’ phone was not the only one that returned to the mainland without its owner, according to the report. Wells’ death attracted national attention and widespread speculation online. The grand jury said allegations targeting the occupants of the three boats involved in the trip had spread to their relatives and friends, calling the "public attacks" "malicious, false," and having "no truth in fact or evidence." Wells’ family was given an opportunity to provide evidence from its private investigation. According to the report, the family’s attorneys said their investigation had found no witnesses or evidence they reasonably believed pointed to potential criminal activity that warranted referral. The case could still return to a grand jury if new evidence emerges. Mississippi has no statute of limitations on homicide cases. Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

articles.title: Sri Lanka Easter attacks: Court finds 15 guilty over deadly bombings
articles.summary: Three churches and three luxury hotels were targeted in the 2019 attacks which killed 270.
articles.body:
Sri Lanka's High Court has convicted 15 men who had been charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500.

Those found guilty include Naufer Moulavi, who prosecutors said masterminded the suicide bombings. Nine other men were acquitted.

The co-ordinated blasts at three churches and three luxury hotels were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Forty-five foreigners were among the dead.

All the bombers who carried out the attacks died in the blasts. Investigators have previously blamed the bombings on Islamist extremists, and the 25 men indicted were from Sri Lanka's Muslim minority. One died in custody.

The court session was adjourned before sentencing.

The accused, who had been charged with more than 23,000 offences, were handcuffed in pairs and brought to the High Court in the capital Colombo in two prison buses.

Most of those killed were Sri Lankans, many of whom were children.

They included celebrity chef Shantha Mayadunne and her daughter, an entire young family of five, at least eight members of staff from the hotels targeted and five members of the same family from the western Sri Lankan city of Negombo.

Among the dead there were also citizens of Australia, Bangladesh, China, Denmark, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.

Three of Danish billionaire Anders Holch Povlsen's children died in the attack on the Shangri-La hotel, while the family had been holidaying there.

In the wake of the attacks, Sri Lankan authorities pointed to a "major intelligence lapse". Its parliament heard that a tip-off from India about the attacks was not properly shared with the authorities.

In 2023, the Supreme Court ordered former president Maithripala Sirisena to pay millions in compensation to the victims of the bombings, after finding him responsible for national security failures that led to the attacks.

Last month, two former senior officials were sentenced to death for criminal negligence that led to the bombings. Death sentences are usually commuted to life in prison in Sri Lanka due to a decades-old moratorium on executions.

For years, Sri Lankans have held regular demonstrations demanding justice for the victims of the Easter attacks.

The verdict comes as a separate investigation into former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is under way. Sallay is accused of orchestrating the bombings with Islamist extremists.

The allegations echo those aired in a 2023 documentary by British broadcaster Channel 4, which heard whistleblower testimony claiming the attacks were allowed to happen to boost the popularity of the Rajapaksa family, which long dominated Sri Lankan politics.

Sallay, who was arrested in February, denies the allegations. Former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was elected months after the 2019 attacks, with a campaign of tackling Islamist extremism has also denied the allegations.

Rajapaksa, who has been banned from leaving the country, has asked the court to prevent his potential arrest in connection with the ongoing investigations.

articles.title: In 2010, a financially ruined couple started farming on leased land; after hitting $100,000 on one-third acre in New York, their farm now pushes nearly $700,000 a year from mostly 2.5 acres
articles.summary: US News: A couple who lost their home in 2010 now earns almost $700,000 a year growing vegetables on just two and a half acres in upstate New York. Corinne Han.
articles.body: A couple who lost their home in 2010 now earns almost $700,000 a year growing vegetables on just two and a half acres in upstate New York. Corinne Hansch and her husband, Matthew Leon, went through serious money trouble during the 2010 recession. When their home in California was about to be taken away, they decided to try growing food for a living. Their first try, in Northern California, fell apart when they lost the land they were renting. So they moved to New York's Capital Region. Starting on just a third of an acre, they built a small but very productive farm. It has since grown into a large local food business with its own store downtown.A rough start in CaliforniaThe couple turned to farming because they had no other choice. In 2010, Leon lost his job and the couple faced losing their house. Speaking on the Real Organic Podcast, Hansch said: "We had nothing to lose, so we might as well start vegetable farming." Leon had studied farming in college, and Hansch grew up on a small farm, but neither of them owned land. They rented an empty field in Mendocino County, California, and used compost to improve the soil. Their small farm did well under a local organic certification group. But after five years, the landowner decided to use the property differently, and the couple had to leave, a problem many new farmers face when they don't own their land.Moving to New YorkThis setback pushed the family to move east, where they could use land owned by relatives. The land sits inside a protected nature preserve about five miles from downtown Amsterdam, New York, and covers 120 acres in total. Hansch and Leon started Lovin' Mama Farm, using 10 acres of the preserve, though most of their crops grow on just two and a half acres. The move changed everything for their business. Mendocino County only had about 90,000 people nearby, but the Capital Region gave them access to more than a million potential customers. In their first year, they had little space and strict rules kept them out of most of the market stalls. At the Troy Waterfront Farmers Market, they were only allowed to sell microgreens at first. "We made $7,000 our first year just selling microgreens," Hansch told the Real Organic Podcast. By the end of their first full year, total sales had already passed $100,000.Building healthy soilMuch of the farm's success comes from years of soil work. The land didn't start with good soil, so they added large amounts of compost. In an interview with public radio station WAMC, Hansch explained: "We've built our soil by adding compost every year between crops... we did that for eight years, until we grew our organic matter in our soil to 12%, which is kind of unheard of in the conventional world." The farm avoids heavy machinery and deep plowing to protect the soil and keep earthworms healthy. Instead, they use light tools that barely disturb the top layer of soil. They also use black tarps and wood chips to block weeds instead of using chemical weed killers. Trees and pastures around the farm act as natural buffers, protecting the crops from chemical drift coming from nearby conventional farms. Ponds and natural habitat nearby support helpful insects, birds, and frogs, cutting down the need for pest control chemicals.Sales grow, and so does the businessToday, Lovin' Mama Farm brings in close to $700,000 a year. Most sales happen directly to customers, through six farmers markets every week, year-round greenhouse growing, and homemade products made from their crops. The farm now has nine greenhouses growing fruit, vegetables, and flowers, with about 12 employees. Even with this success, getting loans has been hard. Hansch told WAMC that securing commercial farm loans remains difficult, so the couple has relied instead on state grants, municipal programs, and direct sales to fund growth.Opening a shop downtownTo bring in more income and help solve local food access problems, the couple opened a retail space in downtown Amsterdam. They rented a 2,100-square-foot storefront near Main Street, turning it into a certified kitchen, market, and café called Lovin' Mama Kitchen. The downtown area has very few grocery stores nearby, so many residents without cars have to travel miles to reach a supermarket. Leon told WAMC: "For 15 years we've been vegetable farming and not had a certified kitchen with which we can turn that product into a value-added item. So, basically, now with a certified kitchen we can take the thousands of pounds of tomatoes that we produce every year and can them into salsa, posadas, tomato sauce." They paid for the new store using several sources: $35,000 raised through crowdfunding, a $35,000 Community Development Block Grant, and another $32,000 from the National Grid Main Street Revitalization Program. The shop sells fresh produce, ready-made meals, and discounted food boxes, and it accepts EBT (food assistance) payments to help lower-income shoppers. "The cool thing is, because we are the farmers, we can really provide things at cost, and we can get really creative... we're really at an advantage because we are the producer," Hansch told WAMC.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Hurricane Polo explodes into rare Category 5 monster after feasting on hot El Niño water
articles.summary: It became one of the fastest intensifying storms on record as El Niño fuels a hyperactive Pacific hurricane season.
articles.body: Hurricane Polo is still strengthening after undergoing extreme rapid intensification and becoming a rare Category 5 on Tuesday morning in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Mexico. ⛈️ Check your local forecast and learn more about hurricanes in the CNN Weather app The 165 mph storm is feeding off of a favorable atmosphere and warmer water driven by the super El Niño, which is fueling a hyperactive hurricane season across the Pacific. More hurricanes are also rapidly intensifying as Earth and its oceans warm from fossil fuel pollution. Extreme rapid intensification is a wind increase of 58 mph or more in 24 hours. Polo met that criteria and then some, with a wind increase of 110 mph, going from a 50 mph tropical storm to a 160 mph Category 5 from Monday to Tuesday morning. This rate of rapid intensification is “truly remarkable,” the National Hurricane Center said Tuesday morning, and is among the fastest on record in the Eastern Pacific. Hurricane Patricia set the Eastern Pacific 24-hour intensification record in 2015 when its winds jumped 120 mph. Polo is comparable to 2023’s Hurricane Otis, which had a wind increase of 105 mph in 21 hours before slamming into and devastating Acapulco, Mexico. Polo was a few hundred miles south-southeast of Manzanillo, Mexico, on Tuesday. Its dangerous hurricane-force winds are forecast to remain offshore as it moves northwestward parallel to the Mexican coastline through the end of the week. The powerful hurricane is moving southeastward right now, but it’s expected to turn to the northwest on Tuesday night. Tropical storm alerts are in effect for Mexico’s southwestern coast since this area is expected to see tropical storm conditions by early Wednesday. Heavy rain is Polo’s most significant impact and it could cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides in this region. Rainfall totals in Guerrero and Michoacán states could reach 3 to 6 inches, with locally up to 8 inches in spots through Thursday. Coastal portions of Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco states could receive 2 to 4 inches of rain. Read more on El Niño

articles.title: Hundreds flee homes in Far North Cameroon after armed group raid kills 15
articles.summary: No group claims responsibility for attack, but suspicion falls on ISIL affiliate.
articles.body:
Hundreds of people have fled their homes after an armed group killed 15 people in the village of Madegoua near the town of Makary in the Far North region of Cameroon.

The attack on Wednesday triggered a wave of displacement from 10 nearby villages. Several hundred people fled towards Kousseri and others went farther afield towards the towns of Mora and Waza close to the border with Nigeria, the RFI news outlet reported.

“They arrived here terrified, sleeping in the open air without food or security,” Mahamat Amadou, a health official in Waza, was quoted as saying by the Africanews outlet.

“Boko Haram asked us to leave our villages. They come to kill us and take our belongings. We are overwhelmed to the point that we have to guard our village from 6pm to 5am,” Kassoum Saley, a displaced resident, told Africanews.

The surge of people arriving in border towns near Nigeria has put pressure on local health services, sparking fears of a humanitarian crisis.

Displaced people said they have not received help from the government, and many women and children have gone days without food.

No group has claimed responsibility for Wednesday’s attack, but a security analyst told the Reuters news agency it was likely carried out by the ISIL (ISIS) affiliate in West Africa ⁠Province, which operates in the area.

Cameroon’s Far North, which borders Nigeria and ‌Chad, has for years been affected by violence involving Boko Haram and other armed groups operating in the Lake Chad ‌Basin.

Cameroon is part of the Multinational Joint Task Force, which is mandated to fight Boko Haram and other armed groups around Lake Chad.

articles.title: Iran delegation to present narrative of resilience, diplomacy at UNGA
articles.summary: Iran’s delegation has arrived to New York for the UNGA where the war with the United States will be raised.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and his team are heading to New York for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) , where they are expected to express grievances about the United States’ war on Iran, but also look at ways of resolving it.

Pezeshkian, who departed Tehran on Tuesday morning local time, is joined by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and other officials, and is scheduled to address the 193-member assembly on Wednesday.

“The issues we will raise at the UN concern expressing the plight of the Iranian nation, the crimes that have been committed against it, and the distrust that has been created,” Pezeshkian told reporters before boarding a flight out of Tehran.

He also warned that the renewed use of force by Iran’s foes would be counterproductive.

“We will make the enemies disappointed,” he said.

Araghchi, who had arrived in New York earlier, said his main goals during meetings on the sidelines will be to “defend the rights and interest of the Iranian people”.

The war started by the US and Israel on Iran on February 28 continues, with disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz that have affected global energy prices.

In the backdrop, Araghchi slammed the UN’s lacklustre performance in establishing peace and security.

“Trust in this organisation has been lost, and this is unfortunately because of its ineffectiveness in establishing international peace and security,” he said.

He said the Minab school bombing by the US and the assassination of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on the opening day of the war would be among the issues Iran will raise at the UN.

Sina Toosi, senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, told Al Jazeera that he believes the Iranian delegation will aim to send a message that it is “open to diplomacy”, but not willing to “de-escalate unilaterally”, as Tehran believes it did in June after the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the US.

“I expect Pezeshkian to present Iran’s current pressure campaign not as an alternative to diplomacy, but as leverage for achieving a more durable agreement,” Toosi said. “The immediate Iranian demands are … an end to the naval blockade, and respect for the Iran-Oman agreement governing transit through Hormuz. In many respects, this amounts to returning to the June understanding and actually implementing it.”

The Iranian delegation will be in New York for five days and is scheduled to return to Tehran on Saturday.

The US has denied visas to Pezeshkian’s accompanying media team and imposed tight restrictions on their movement in the country, according to the president’s office. Iranian delegates will also be barred from buying luxury goods during their stay.

Still, Pezeshkian plans to hold discussions with Iranian expatriates, intellectuals, think tanks and media in the coming days.

The UNGA brings together representatives of nearly 130 countries at the body’s headquarters in New York.

This year’s assembly, which begins on Tuesday, comes as the US tightens economic pressure through sanctions and a naval blockade on southern Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz.

US President Donald Trump said earlier this week that he was considering a new major military assault on Iran, but wanted to hear from the Arab leaders of the region first. He is set to meet with representatives from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait and Bahrain in the coming days to discuss the war on Iran.

This and a military escalation in Yemen, where Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces are fighting the Iran-aligned Ansar Allah, also known as the Houthis, are other concerns for the assembly.

The Houthis have expanded control over the strait of Bab al-Mandeb in recent weeks after making rapid military advances in western Yemen and the Red Sea coast.

Regional mediators – including Pakistan, Qatar, Oman and Turkiye – have pushed for a diplomatic end to the crisis amid prospects of escalated conflict.

As Iran demands a return to the memorandum of understanding signed with the US in June to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, its diplomats are expected to sit down with mediators in New York as well.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera earlier this week that Tehran has communicated seven conditions to the US to reopen the strategic waterway.

These included an end to war on all fronts, the release of Iran’s frozen assets, the lifting of the blockade on Iranian ports, an end to military attacks on Iranian territory, and noninterference in the country’s internal affairs. But he also said Iran remains prepared for escalated fighting, and could potentially abandon the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) depending on future US actions.

Toosi told Al Jazeera that there was a “real opening” for diplomacy, but “no guarantee of a breakthrough”.

“The fundamental obstacle is credibility,” Toosi said. “Tehran’s conclusion from the June MoU was that de-escalating first left it dependent on US commitments that Washington could reverse or simply fail to implement. That helps explain why Iran is now trying to negotiate while maintaining coercive leverage, particularly over Hormuz.”

“The UN therefore presents a potentially important opportunity because both sides have reasons to explore an off-ramp,” Toosi added. The question is whether Trump is prepared to negotiate a genuinely reciprocal agreement, rather than treating diplomacy as a mechanism for Iran to surrender its leverage first.”

Meanwhile, in Iran, there are conflicting views about how to end the war with the US, with some parties open to a peaceful resolution and more hardline factions seeking to continue or intensify the war until all Tehran’s demands are met.

Hossein Mohebbi, the spokesman of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), told local media on Tuesday that Iran was prepared to use new weapons systems against the US if necessary, and pointed to its recent attacks on US warships .

But he added that the country was open to peace. “If our national interests call for it to conduct some negotiations alongside war, we must negotiate,” he said.

Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator, had already said both options remain on the table, but said hardline factions have no end date for the war of attrition. Other factions underestimate Iran’s capabilities and believe it must surrender, he said.

“The first keeps the country in a state of perpetual crisis and the other offers national resources and dignity to the enemy on a platter,” Ghalibaf said. “Both approaches realise the enemy’s wish for disturbing the country’s cohesion and unity.”

Trump said on Sunday he would “probably be open” to meeting Pezeshkian in New York, although the Iranian government’s IRNA news service dismissed this as a “new propaganda game”.

The government’s daily Iran newspaper said New York could offer a “platform for the Iranian narrative”. The hardline Kayhan newspaper wanted Pezeshkian to turn the UN into “a courtroom for American crimes”.

Public expectations in Iran are sceptical that the UN meetings will produce any political breakthrough to end the war, which has deepened the average Iranian citizen’s economic woes .

“I think Pezeshkian going [to New York] is better than him not going, but there is no hope that anything comes of it,” one Iranian told Al Jazeera in western Tehran, on condition of anonymity due to security concerns.

Another resident of the capital also said she harboured no hopes of a diplomatic resolution.

“I think if [the politicians] want to, then yes, there can be an opening, but they don’t want to,” she said.

articles.title: Mum and three children die in Bootle house fire
articles.summary: Another person was taken to hospital following the "intense fire which spread very rapidly".
articles.body:
A mother and three children have died in a house fire on Merseyside.

Six fire engines were at the scene at the height of the blaze at the semi-detached property in Stone Square in Bootle, Sefton, at 03:45 BST.

Eight firefighters searched the house where they discovered four people in an upstairs bedroom who were showing no signs of life, Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said.

Another casualty, who was outside the property when crews arrived, was taken to hospital.

Officers from Merseyside Police were at the scene and a joint investigation with the fire service into the cause of the blaze is under way.

The North West Ambulance Service's hazardous area response team also attended the scene of the fire and confirmed the four fatalities.

Chief Fire Officer Nick Searle confirmed the "intense fire [had] spread very rapidly".

The street was cordoned off by police and, earlier, fire officers could be seen knocking on neighbours' doors.

One said: "I heard shouting in the early hours but I just thought someone was having an argument, then I came downstairs and saw all the fire engines."

Another local resident, who did not want to be named, said: "We all came out on the front and we could see smoke coming over from the houses.

"The sirens woke me up and there were fire engines in the street."

The fire service said the main blaze had been extinguished with crews damping down the area.

Kevin Longshaw, area manager for Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service, said: "This is a devastating incident, and our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of those who have lost their lives and been injured.

"We will work closely with relevant colleagues to ascertain the cause of the fire, but in the immediate term, we again extend our sincere condolences to those affected by this tragic incident."

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer asks judge to investigate juror and check his phone
articles.summary: The attorney wants the court to look at the juror's mobile phone use and answers on questionnaires.
articles.body:
The defence lawyer for a Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three children has asked a judge to investigate a juror in the case.

The proceedings against Lindsay Clancy ended in a mistrial and acrimony this month after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict.

Her attorney, Kevin Reddington, wants the court to probe mobile phone use by "Juror Doe" during deliberations as well as a questionnaire he filled out.

A lawyer for Michael Desronvil, the lone juror who wanted to find Clancy guilty, said the latest defence motion was a "Looney Tunes" attack on his client for doing his civic duty. Desronvil has said there was "enough proof that she [Clancy] knew exactly what she was doing".

Warning: This article contains distressing details

The juror forewoman has claimed in a media interview that Desronvil had expressed reasonable doubt about Clancy's guilt, which would require him to find her not guilty. He denies this.

Clancy has not denied killing her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home.

Her attorneys argued she was not guilty by reason of insanity, that she was struggling with postpartum psychosis at the time.

Prosecutors said Clancy made a calculated decision to send her husband out of the house on an errand so she could strangle her children.

In his motion filed on Friday, Reddington asked the court to look at calls and texts that "Juror Doe" made between 08:00 and 16:30 local time during all the days the jury deliberated.

He also asked the court to examine the truthfulness of the answers the juror gave during the jury selection process, as well as his responses to prospective juror questionnaires.

In a separate motion, Reddington also asked for the case against Clancy to be dismissed. Prosecutors have yet to say whether they will retry her.

Facing a backlash for refusing to acquit Clancy, Desronvil has hired an attorney to represent him.

The lawyer, Edward Paltzik, said in a statement on X that the "disgusting" defence motion was an attack on the US constitutional right to a fair trial.

"If the new normal is that jurors are going to face brutal reprisals for disagreeing with a defense attorney, you can kiss the Sixth Amendment goodbye," he wrote.

Several jurors have said after the trial ended that they were ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible.

Desronvil said last week that he had no doubt about her guilt.

"As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented," he said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

The jury forewoman, a retired fifth-grade teacher, said in an interview with NBC that Desronvil had admitted he had reasonable doubt, but refused to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity.

articles.title: Rajya Sabha polls for 12 seats: BJP likely to retain 8 in UP, SP eyes gain, BSP at risk
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The BJP is set to have the numbers on its side in the upcoming Rajya Sabha elections in Uttar Pradesh, with the party-led alliance expected.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The BJP is set to have the numbers on its side in the upcoming Rajya Sabha elections in Uttar Pradesh, with the party-led alliance expected to win eight of the 10 seats going to polls in the state. The Samajwadi Party could take the remaining two seats, based on the current strength of parties in the assembly.The Election Commission on Tuesday announced polls for 12 Rajya Sabha seats in Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand and West Bengal. Voting, if required, will be held on October 16, with the results also to be declared the same day.The BJP is also expected to add one seat to its Rajya Sabha tally by winning the lone seat from West Bengal. The seat became vacant after actor Rukmini Mallick, popularly known as Koel, resigned from the House. The Trinamool Congress had sent her to the Rajya Sabha before losing power in the assembly election held earlier this year.In Uttar Pradesh, the BJP-led alliance has around 290 MLAs, while the SP-Congress combine has about 103. A candidate needs around 37 votes to win a Rajya Sabha seat.The BJP can comfortably win seven seats, while the SP-Congress combine can secure two. The contest for the 10th seat could be closer, with the BJP-led alliance starting with around 31 votes against around 29 for the SP-Congress side.The polls could also mark the end of the BSP's representation in Parliament. Mayawati's party has no member in the Lok Sabha and its only MLA in Uttar Pradesh, Uma Shankar Singh, died in August. The term of BSP's lone Rajya Sabha member, Ramji Gautam, ends in November.Gautam is among the nine Uttar Pradesh members whose terms are ending. The others are Union minister Hardeep Singh Puri, BJP leaders Arun Singh, Geeta Shakya, Neeraj Shekhar, Brijlal, B L Verma and Seema Dwivedi, and SP leader Ram Gopal Yadav.Puri's continuation in the Union Cabinet will depend on whether the BJP nominates him for another Rajya Sabha term.The 10th Uttar Pradesh seat was held by former deputy chief minister Dinesh Sharma. It became vacant earlier this month after Sharma resigned from the Rajya Sabha following his appointment as lieutenant governor of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.The BSP had managed to retain its Rajya Sabha presence in 2020 after the BJP fielded only eight candidates for 10 seats. The move allowed the BSP and SP to each elect one member unopposed.Gautam was elected unopposed after the nomination of an SP-backed Independent candidate was rejected. The SP had then alleged an understanding between the BJP and BSP.In Uttarakhand, BJP Rajya Sabha member Naresh Bansal's term is ending. The BJP, which has a comfortable majority in the state assembly, is expected to retain the seat.The election notification will be issued on September 29. articles.title: Tim Westwood charged with two more sexual offences
articles.summary: The alleged sexual offences date back to 1991 and 2004.
articles.body:
Former BBC Radio 1 and Capital Xtra DJ Tim Westwood has been charged with two more offences, the Metropolitan Police have said.

The charges are an alleged indecent assault against a teenage girl aged 16 to 17 in Hammersmith and Fulham in 1991 and the alleged sexual assault of an 18-year-old woman in Wandsworth in 2004.

These charges are in addition to those brought against Westwood, 68, in October 2025 relating to seven women, which include four counts of rape.

Westwood has previously denied multiple sex offences, including rape and sexual assault, and pleaded not guilty to earlier charges last December.

Westwood is now facing a total of 17 charges involving nine women.

Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from the Metropolitan Police Service, said: "The women who have made reports have placed their trust in us, and we remain committed to providing them with all available support.

"Independent support is also available through Rape Crisis via its 24/7 Rape and Sexual Abuse Support Line."

Westwood is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court at a future date in relation to the two additional charges, the Met Police said.

A trial relating to the original 15 charges is scheduled to begin at Southwark Crown Court on 25 January 2027.

Catherine P Baccas, deputy chief crown prosecutor in the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) London, said: "Today the Crown Prosecution Service has authorised two further charges of sexual assault and indecent assault against Tim Westwood.

"Mr Westwood is already charged with nine counts of indecent assault, two counts of sexual assault and four counts of rape in relation to reported non-recent offences between 1983 and 2016 involving seven women.

"These new charges, following an investigation by the Metropolitan Police, relate to separate reports of non-recent offences in 1991 and 2004 involving two additional women.

"Our prosecutors have worked to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring these additional charges to court and that it is in the public interest to pursue further criminal proceedings.

"The Crown Prosecution Service reminds everyone that criminal proceedings are active, and the defendant has the right to a fair trial."

articles.title: Veteran BBC Africa correspondent Mark Doyle dies
articles.summary: Doyle was best known for reporting on African conflicts in the 1990s and 2000s, notably in Rwanda and Sierra Leone.
articles.body:
British journalist Mark Doyle, best known for his reporting on conflicts in Africa in the 1990s and 2000s, has died aged 67 after a short illness.

After living in Africa, he joined the BBC in 1986. Doyle became East Africa correspondent in 1993 and made his mark covering the Rwandan genocide a year later.

As West Africa correspondent from 1997 to 2002, he reported on Sierra Leone's brutal civil war and aftermath of Liberia's conflict.

Following Doyle's death, BBC foreign editor Paul Danahar said he was a "legendary figure", as well as a" brilliant, brave, empathetic reporter".

The BBC's Andrew Harding, who worked with Doyle, paid tribute to his former colleague in a 2015 article, published to mark his departure from the national broadcaster.

In the piece Fergal Keane, another prominent BBC correspondent in Africa, recalled their stint in Rwanda in 1994. "He stayed longer than any of us," Keane said of Doyle. "Those who were in that awful place at that awful time will know what Mark Doyle gave for the cause of truth and for the BBC."

In the same article Sir David Richards, who headed British forces struggling to stop Sierra Leone's civil war in 2000, also praised Doyle.

Sir David said his reporting helped convince the UK government of the need for a robust intervention. "Hence the saving of thousands of Sierra Leonean lives that would otherwise have been at huge risk," he said.

In 2004 Doyle won first prize in the UN Correspondents Association/UN Foundation Awards for his coverage of post-war Liberia.

He became BBC World Affairs correspondent before retiring from the BBC in 2015.

articles.title: Sri Lanka court convicts 15 men over 2019 Easter Sunday bombings
articles.summary: South Asia News: A Sri Lankan court on Tuesday found 15 men guilty of involvement in the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings that killed more than 260 people and wounded about.
articles.body: A Sri Lankan court on Tuesday found 15 men guilty of involvement in the 2019 Easter Sunday bombings that killed more than 260 people and wounded about 500.The coordinated attacks targeted three churches and three hotels across the island nation during Easter services and celebrations.The Islamic State-inspired bombings were among the deadliest attacks in Sri Lanka's history. Forty-two foreigners were among those killed, according to the news agency Associated Press.The verdict comes more than seven years after the April 21, 2019 attacks, as separate investigations into the circumstances surrounding the bombings continue.15 convicted, nine acquittedThe high court convicted 15 men who had been charged with plotting the attacks, while nine others were acquitted. The accused faced more than 23,000 charges, including murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and offences involving firearms and explosives.Prosecutors said Naufer Moulavi, one of those convicted, masterminded the suicide bombings, the BBC reported.More than 2,300 people gave evidence for the prosecution, while investigators presented 2,076 pieces of evidence, including explosives, swords and firearms.None of the people believed to have directly carried out the bombings survived. The coordinated blasts at three churches and three hotels were attributed to two Sri Lanka-based Islamic militant groups.Death sentences and earlier convictionsAuthorities filed 23,270 charges against 24 suspects in 2021 over allegations that they planned or inspired the attacks.The charges were brought under the Prevention of Terrorism Act and included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism, and firearms and explosives offences.Sri Lanka has not carried out an execution since 1976. As a result, death sentences are typically followed by life imprisonment.In July, a former police chief and a former senior defence ministry official were sentenced to death for failing to act promptly on foreign intelligence warnings about possible attacks.The two former senior officials were sentenced for criminal negligence linked to the bombings.Questions over intelligence failuresThe attacks prompted questions over security and intelligence failures. Sri Lankan authorities identified a major intelligence lapse, while parliament heard that a warning from India about possible attacks had not been properly shared with the authorities.In 2023, Sri Lanka's Supreme Court ordered former president Maithripala Sirisena to pay compensation to victims after finding him responsible for national security failures that contributed to the attacks.Sri Lanka's Catholic Church has also alleged, without providing evidence, that those identified as perpetrators were not the masterminds and that a wider conspiracy was behind the attacks, according to AP.Separate investigation into former intelligence chiefA separate investigation involving former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is also underway.Sallay is accused of orchestrating the bombings with Islamist extremists and denies the allegations.The claims echo allegations aired in a 2023 Channel 4 documentary, which included whistleblower testimony alleging that the attacks were allowed to happen to boost the popularity of the Rajapaksa family, which had long dominated Sri Lankan politics.Former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was elected months after the attacks after campaigning on tackling Islamist extremism, has denied the allegations.He has been banned from leaving the country and has asked a court to prevent his potential arrest in connection with the ongoing investigation.For years, Sri Lankans have held demonstrations demanding justice for those killed and injured in the Easter Sunday attacks.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Where is the US opening new military bases in Greenland?
articles.summary: At least two new US bases will be established as part of a deal with Denmark and Greenland.
articles.body:
The US will open two military bases in Greenland as part of a deal with Denmark and Greenland, Reuters has reported.

The agreement is expected to be signed on Tuesday at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York. However, its text has not yet been officially publicised.

The move follows a tense, months-long standoff with Denmark and Greenland following US President Donald Trump’s repeated comments that Washington intended to annex the autonomous Danish territory, which is strategic for its location in the Arctic and its significant mineral resources, including rare-earth metals.

As a diplomatic row brewed last year, Trump refused to rule out a military invasion, causing fear among Greenlanders, the majority of whom reject US control according to polls.

Tensions peaked in January this year when European members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) alliance began deploying more troops to the island to demonstrate military readiness and to deter Washington.

Following talks with NATO chief Mark Rutte, Trump backed down, saying he would not invade the island but would, instead, work towards a deal. He also withdrew his threat to impose 10 percent trade tariffs on eight European nations objecting to the US’s attempts to acquire Greenland.

Greenland and Denmark then began negotiations with the US to de-escalate the crisis. Here’s what we know:

On Friday, US President Donald Trump claimed the US had reached a deal with Denmark granting it “permanent control” over Greenland’s security “and all other needs”.

The deal allows the US a veto to prevent “adversaries” from establishing a military presence or making “sensitive investments” in Greenland without its approval, Trump said.

A US Department of State official cited by the BBC clarified that will mean non-NATO states will not be able to set up bases in Greenland and will be barred from “making investments in Greenland that could threaten the United States”.

Then, on Monday, news of the two new US bases emerged.

Over the weekend, Denmark and Greenland confirmed they had reached an agreement with the US that would be announced this week, but insisted that it would not compromise Greenland’s sovereignty.

In a post on Facebook, Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said, “The agreement recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination.”

On Monday, in advance of the deal’s signing, Nielsen added that it would be a “significant moment following a difficult period … I look forward to signing the agreement and taking the next step with our interests, our security, and respect for our country as the clear starting point.”

Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen also sounded an optimistic note in a weekend statement.

“A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security ‌in the Arctic and the north Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within Nato Europe – while respecting the Danish kingdom’s red lines,” Rasmussen said.

The US will re-establish one Cold War-era military base in southern Greenland, and set up another on the east coast under the coming deal, it has been reported.

The first base will be in Narsarsuaq, a settlement in southern Greenland whose population has dwindled to a few dozen people since the US closed its Bluie West One military base – also known as Narsarsuaq Air Base and Narsarsuaq Airport – in 1958.

The second base will be located in Mestersvig, a military outpost in the northeast of the territory that is currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish special forces unit.

The US maintained a heavy military presence on the island during the Cold War when American nuclear bombers and nuclear early warning systems were based there. Some 150 troops remain permanently at the northern Pituffik Space Base monitoring for missiles.

What have the reactions been to the US deal?

Trump has argued that taking control of the island, which is on the most direct route between North America and Europe, is necessary to prevent Russia and China from ramping up their own presence in the Arctic, near the US’s northern border.

Analysts say that neither country has significant influence in the region. Nevertheless, the proposed deal stipulated that the US’s adversaries cannot similarly have any Greenland bases.

Russia, responding to the agreement, has said that it was not involved in discussions.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Tuesday that “at present, the issue of cooperation in the Arctic is not on the agenda. The Americans and other Arctic states are refusing to cooperate with Russia.”

Earlier, over the weekend, a NATO spokesperson told reporters that the alliance was on board with the deal and said it would “help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region”.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Pakistan needs to take credible action against cross-border terrorism before the world can believe what it says, the ministry of external affairs said on Tuesday, while hitting out at Islamabad over its claims regarding a recent decision by the Permanent Court of Arbitration.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal accused Pakistan of “misrepresenting facts” and spreading “falsehoods” as part of its propaganda.“Pakistan has a habit of misrepresenting facts and propagating falsehoods to serve its malicious propaganda,” Jaiswal said.“For starters, the so-called ruling is not a ruling by the Permanent Court of Arbitration, as sought to be projected by the Pakistan minister. It is a ruling by an illegally constituted court. We see this as just one more attempt by Pakistan at distorting the reality,” he added.Jaiswal was responding to a question about Pakistan circulating a letter to the president of the UN Security Council regarding recent rulings related to the Permanent Court of Arbitration.His comments also came days after Pakistan increased the reward for information leading to the arrest or conviction of Jaish-e-Mohammed (JeM) chief Masood Azhar.India had last week described Pakistan's PKR 70 lakh reward for information on Azhar as a “phoney” move and asked Islamabad to take concrete action against the JeM chief.The Pakistan-based Jaish-e-Mohammed has been linked to several major terror attacks in India, including the 2001 Parliament attack and the attacks in Pathankot and Pulwama.The group was founded by most-wanted terrorist Masood Azhar.New Delhi has repeatedly called on Pakistan to take credible action against crossborder terrorism, saying Islamabad's actions would be a key test of the credibility of its claims.India seeks constructive ties with BangladeshOn India-Bangladesh relations, Jaiswal said New Delhi wants positive and constructive ties with Dhaka.“India seeks positive, constructive and forward-looking ties with Bangladesh,” he said.275 Indians missing in NepalOn Indians missing in Nepal floods, Jaiswal said an Indian forensic team was working with Nepalese authorities to identify those still unaccounted for.“As I told you last time, we had given you a figure of 275 Indian nationals who were missing. Over and above that, several other people from the Indian diaspora and persons of Indian origin are also missing,” he said.“We have a forensic team in Nepal that is working in Kathmandu in several laboratories along with their Nepali colleagues,” Jaiswal said.He said the Indian team was working on 3,000 samples and had so far arrived at more than 1,200 DNA profiles.“The work is going on, and regarding the missing Indian nationals and missing persons, we await to hear from the Nepali authorities,” he said.India reiterates dialogue, diplomacy on UkraineOn the Ukraine conflict, Jaiswal said external affairs minister S Jaishankar met Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha on Monday and discussed recent developments.“Yes, the external affairs minister met with the Ukrainian foreign minister yesterday. During the meeting, he discussed the recent developments in the conflict,” Jaiswal said.Jaishankar reiterated India's position that dialogue and diplomacy are the way forward for a peaceful resolution.“The external affairs minister once again put forth India's point that dialogue and diplomacy are the way forward for a peaceful resolution,” Jaiswal said.“India, as you know, is in touch with both sides, Ukraine and Russia, and we have told them that if there is any way that India can contribute, India is ready to do so,” he added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Inquest opens into 'Putney Pusher' suspect's death
articles.summary: Nicholas Brandram, who was suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a bus, was found dead last week.
articles.body:
A man suspected of knocking a woman into the path of a bus on Putney Bridge was found dead by his brother-in-law after missing a family meal, his inquest has heard.

Nicholas Brandram, 44, was discovered at his home in Chiswick on 15 September, West London Coroner's Court was told.

He had been arrested in June on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm in relation to the incident of May 2017, when a woman was shoved into the road by a jogger. His family say he was not involved.

Opening and adjourning the inquest, West London coroner Melanie Lee said she had been told of a referral to the Independent Office of Police Conduct and was suspending the hearing pending the outcome of its inquiry.

The coroner offered her "sincere condolences" to Brandram's family, in particular his sisters Sophie Voelcker and Alexia Hicks who were at the hearing in Fulham.

The court heard that Brandram's brother-in-law used a spare key provided by a neighbour and found the married banker in an upstairs room.

Paramedics attended but despite their resuscitation efforts he was pronounced dead just before 21:00 BST. Police did not regard the death as suspicious or believe there had been any third-party involvement, the inquest heard.

Brandram's family have insisted he was not the jogger, referred to as the Putney Pusher in media coverage at the time, and blame the Met Police's handling of the case for his death.

They said last week that he "took his own life after months of immense pressure caused by a Metropolitan Police investigation", and there was no forensic evidence linking the banker to the incident.

The force said it recognised the "strain that being subject to a police investigation" could cause.
